formation.title: The Land of the Pharaohs Reborn
formation.text:
Egypt stands united once more under a single banner. For millennia this land has been the crossroads of empires, the granary that fed Rome, the fortress that turned back the Mongols, the market where East met West. The Nile still flows, the harvests still come, and now a new question confronts us: shall Egypt's destiny be written in the language of the sword, or in the ledgers of the counting house? Our Mamluk cavalry remain the finest horsemen in the world, their furusiyya tradition unbroken across centuries. Yet the riches of the Nile valley (cotton, grain, sugar, spices flowing through our ports) offer a different kind of power. The choice before us will define what Egypt becomes.

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: We are the heirs of Baybars. Let our enemies tremble!

modifiers.name: Sword of the Sultan
modifiers.text: The Mamluk military tradition lives on. Our cavalry charges shake the earth and our armies march with the discipline of centuries. Egypt's sword is drawn, and none shall stand before it.

options.text: The Nile provides. Let our prosperity be our shield.

modifiers.name: Garden of the Nile
modifiers.text: The Nile's bounty is the foundation of our prosperity. Rich harvests feed a growing nation, trade flows through our markets, and the wealth of ages past fuels the ambitions of ages to come.

advances.name: Furusiyya Tradition
advances.text: The Mamluk art of horsemanship, archery, and mounted combat, passed down through generations of elite slave-soldiers.

advances.name: Nile Irrigation Systems
advances.text: The ancient basin irrigation systems of the Nile, enhanced with saqiya water wheels and shaduf lifting devices.

advances.name: Wikala Trade Network
advances.text: A network of urban caravanserais providing lodging, storage, and commercial facilities for long-distance merchants.

advances.name: Mamluk Administration
advances.text: The sophisticated bureaucratic system developed by the Mamluk sultans to govern Egypt and its provinces.

advances.name: Legacy of the Pharaohs
advances.text: The weight of five thousand years of civilization lends Egypt an unmatched cultural authority and prestige.

advances.name: Slave Soldier Tradition
advances.text: The practice of training purchased slaves into elite soldiers, creating a military caste of unmatched loyalty and discipline.

advances.name: Nile River Fleet
advances.text: Shallow-draft galleys designed for patrol and transport along the Nile and in the coastal waters of the Mediterranean and Red Sea.

advances.name: Revival of Al-Azhar
advances.text: The restoration and expansion of Al-Azhar as the foremost center of Sunni Islamic scholarship in the world.

event.title: The Revival of Al-Azhar
event.text: Since its founding by the Fatimids in 970, Al-Azhar has been a beacon of Islamic learning. Under Mamluk patronage, the mosque-university grew into the foremost center of Sunni scholarship in the world. Waqf endowments fund halls of study where jurists debate questions of law, astronomers chart the heavens, and physicians advance the art of healing. Students arrive from Andalusia, from Persia, from the distant lands of the Sahel, drawn by Al-Azhar's reputation. Now, with Egyptian sovereignty restored, we may elevate this ancient institution to even greater heights. Shall we invest in its scholarly mission, or channel its prestige toward the stability of the state?

options.text: Al-Azhar shall be the lamp of the world.

modifiers.name: Light of Al-Azhar
modifiers.text: Al-Azhar's scholars illuminate the Islamic world with their learning, drawing students from every corner of the faith. Egypt stands as the intellectual heart of civilization.

options.text: Let Al-Azhar guide the faithful with renewed authority.

modifiers.name: Al-Azhar's Authority
modifiers.text: Al-Azhar's renewed prestige draws scholars from across the Islamic world, lending religious legitimacy to the state and fostering a culture of learning and jurisprudence.

advances.name: Cairo Madrasas
advances.text: A network of religious schools founded and endowed by the Mamluk elite, spreading literacy and Islamic learning.

advances.name: Egyptian Cotton
advances.text: The cultivation and processing of Egypt's prized long-staple cotton, a crop that would become the foundation of the modern Egyptian economy. In the weaving towns of the Delta it is spun and woven fine for export.

advances.name: Sultanic Diplomacy
advances.text: The sophisticated diplomatic tradition of the Egyptian sultanate, balancing relations between Christendom, the Mongol khanates, and rival Muslim powers.

advances.name: Granary of the East
advances.text: Egypt's role as the breadbasket of the eastern Mediterranean, exporting grain to feed the cities of the region.

advances.name: Suez Transit Trade
advances.text: Control of the land bridge between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, the shortest route between Europe and the riches of Asia.

event.title: Gateway Between the Seas
event.text: Egypt has always been the hinge between two worlds. To our north, the Mediterranean connects us to Europe and the riches of Christendom. To our east, the Red Sea opens the road to India, the Spice Islands, and the wealth of the Orient. Caravans cross the isthmus of Suez carrying pepper and silk, coffee and incense, in quantities that would stagger the imagination of lesser nations. Our warehouses at the ports of Suez and Alexandria bulge with the goods of three continents. The revenue from this transit trade alone could fund a kingdom. We stand at the crossroads of the world, and every merchant who passes through our land enriches Egypt.

advances.name: Egyptian Sipahi
advances.text: Heavy cavalry lancers in the tradition of the Ottoman sipahi, adapted to Egyptian conditions and the Mamluk heritage of mounted warfare.

advances.name: Spice Entrepot
advances.text: Egypt's position as the central warehouse for the spice trade, where pepper, cinnamon, and cloves change hands between Eastern producers and Western buyers.

advances.name: Citadel Tradition
advances.text: The tradition of monumental fortress construction dating back to Saladin's Citadel of Cairo, providing Egypt with formidable defensive capabilities.

advances.name: Nile Sugar Industry
advances.text: The processing of sugar cane grown along the Nile, an industry that once made Egypt a major sugar exporter to the Mediterranean world. The cane is crushed in ox-turned presses and the juice boiled and set in clay cones.

advances.name: Waqf Endowment System
advances.text: The system of charitable religious endowments that funds mosques, madrasas, hospitals, and public works across Egypt.

advances.name: Egyptian Janissary Garrison
advances.text: Disciplined infantry garrison troops modeled on the Ottoman janissary system, maintaining order in Egypt's cities and fortresses.

advances.name: Grand Bazaar of Cairo
advances.text: The expansion of Cairo's Khan al-Khalili and surrounding bazaar districts into a sprawling commercial complex rivaling any market in the world.

advances.name: Iltizam Tax Farming
advances.text: The system of auctioning tax collection rights to the highest bidder, providing immediate revenue to the state at the cost of provincial autonomy.

advances.name: Egyptian Coffee Culture
advances.text: The coffeehouses of Cairo become centers of social life, commerce, and intellectual exchange, fueled by beans imported through the Red Sea trade.

advances.name: Felucca Patrol Fleet
advances.text: A fleet of fast, lateen-rigged feluccas for coastal patrol, river transport, and light naval operations.

advances.name: Egyptian Sufi Orders
advances.text: The powerful Sufi brotherhoods of Egypt, the Shadhiliyya, Ahmadiyya, and others, whose lodges provide spiritual guidance and social cohesion.

advances.name: Nizam-i Jedid
advances.text: The New Order, a modern professional army trained in European tactics, equipped with locally manufactured weapons, and led by academy-trained officers.

event.title: The New Order
event.text: The old Mamluk military system, for all its glorious history, cannot contend with the disciplined armies of Europe. Egyptian students sent abroad have returned with knowledge of drill manuals, modern tactics, and organizational methods that transform raw peasant conscripts into professional soldiers. The Nizam-i Jedid, the New Order, represents nothing less than a revolution in Egyptian military affairs. Factories in Cairo now produce muskets and cannons to European standards. A military academy trains officers in the science of war. The transformation is painful and costly, but the alternative is subjugation. Egypt shall have a modern army, or Egypt shall have no army at all.

options.text: Egypt shall stand among the great military powers.

modifiers.name: Egyptian Renaissance
modifiers.text: A new army drilled in modern tactics, factories rising along the Nile, and a generation of officers trained in the arts of war. Egypt awakens to its destiny among the great powers.

options.text: Modernize the economy, not just the army.

modifiers.name: Economic Modernization
modifiers.text: The New Order extends beyond the barracks. Factories, modern workshops, and reformed trade practices transform Egypt's economy alongside its military.

advances.name: Cairo Arsenal
advances.text: A state weapons manufactory producing muskets, cannons, and ammunition to equip the modernized Egyptian army.

advances.name: Cotton Monopoly
advances.text: State control of the lucrative long-staple cotton trade, with Egyptian cotton commanding premium prices in European textile markets.

advances.name: Centralized Pashalik
advances.text: The transformation of Egypt from a loosely governed Ottoman province into a centralized state with direct control over its provinces and resources.

advances.name: Corvee Labor System
advances.text: The mobilization of peasant labor for great public works, canals, dams, roads, and fortifications, the same system that once built the pyramids. Deep canals are dug to carry water at low Nile, and cleared of silt by the villages every year.

advances.name: Bulaq Printing Press
advances.text: The first printing press in the Arab world, established at Bulaq in Cairo, producing Arabic books on military science, medicine, and engineering.

advances.name: Modern Egyptian Army
advances.text: A fully modernized infantry force drilled in European line tactics, equipped with percussion-cap muskets, and organized into brigades and divisions.

advances.name: Egyptian Industrialization
advances.text: State-owned factories producing textiles, weapons, and processed goods, part of the ambitious program to transform Egypt into an industrial power.

advances.name: Egyptian School of Medicine
advances.text: A modern medical school in Cairo, training physicians in European surgical techniques and public health practices.

advances.name: Suez Transit Revenues
advances.text: The immense revenue generated by controlling the shortest trade route between Europe and Asia, as the isthmus becomes the busiest commercial corridor in the world.

advances.name: Peasant Conscription
advances.text: The mass conscription of Egyptian peasants into the national army, transforming the fellahin into soldiers of the state.

advances.name: Egyptian National Awakening
advances.text: The emergence of an Egyptian national consciousness distinct from Ottoman imperial identity, driven by shared language, history, and the experience of modernization.

destiny.name: Egyptian Destiny
destiny.text: Egypt stands at a crossroads. Shall the pharaohs' heirs pursue the sword or the plough? The destiny of the Nile awaits.

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: Egypt's Destiny Beckons
event.text: The formation of Egypt is complete, but the work has only begun. Before us lie two roads, one paved with the victories of the sword, the other lined with the gold of commerce and the green of the Nile's harvest. Our ancestors built monuments that have endured five thousand years. Whatever path we choose, let our deeds echo just as long.

options.text: Our destiny is written in the stars above the Nile.

destiny.name: Reconquest of the Levant
destiny.text: Jerusalem and Damascus are secured and three garrison towns are given their barracks, restoring Egypt's dominion over the eastern Mediterranean lands that the Mamluks once held.

conditions.text: Chose Sword of the Sultan
Own Jerusalem, or a subject owns it
Own Damascus, or a subject owns it
At least 3 of our locations have a Mamluk Barracks

event.title: The Eagle Returns to the Levant
event.text: Egyptian banners fly once more over the holy city of Jerusalem and the ancient walls of Damascus. The Mamluk sultans of old, Baybars, Qalawun, al-Nasir, would recognize the ambition that drives us. The Levantine coast, that contested shore where Crusaders and Mongols once broke against Egyptian resolve, is ours again. Our garrison commanders report the cities secured, the trade routes reopened, and the local population adjusting to Egyptian administration. The sultan's writ runs from the Nile delta to the Syrian steppe.

options.text: The Levant bows to the sultan once more.

destiny.name: Heart of Islam
destiny.text: Custody of the Holy Cities of Mecca and Medina is taken and Baghdad, seat of the ancient caliphate, is seized. The renown of it makes Egypt the undisputed center of the Islamic world.

conditions.text: Own Mecca, or a subject owns it
Own Baghdad, or a subject owns it
Own Madīna, or a subject owns it
Prestige at least 50

event.title: Guardian of the Two Sanctuaries
event.text: The conquest of Mecca, Medina and Baghdad places Egypt at the very heart of the Islamic world. The custodianship of the Holy Cities confers a religious authority that transcends mere temporal power, while control of Baghdad, once the seat of the Abbasid caliphate, stakes Egypt's claim to be the successor of that ancient institution. The question now is how to wield this extraordinary position. Shall we emphasize our role as military guardian, projecting force to protect the faithful? Or shall we claim the mantle of caliphal legitimacy, using diplomacy and prestige to build a network of loyal subjects?

options.text: We shall guard the faithful with our armies.

modifiers.name: Guardian of the Holy Cities
modifiers.text: Egypt's armies stand watch over the sacred sites of Islam, projecting military power to defend the faithful and enforce the sultan's authority across the Middle East.

options.text: We claim the legacy of the Abbasid caliphs.

modifiers.name: Heir of the Abbasids
modifiers.text: Egypt claims the diplomatic and spiritual legacy of the Abbasid caliphate, wielding religious prestige and political influence to bind the Islamic world to Cairo's will.

destiny.name: The Sultan's Domain
destiny.text: Egyptian sovereignty is extended from Aleppo to Aden and six towns are garrisoned from their own barracks, so that every route between the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean is commanded under the sultan's banner.

conditions.text: Own Aleppo, or a subject owns it
Own 'Adan, or a subject owns it
Prestige at least 75
Gold at least 3000
At least 6 of our locations have a Mamluk Barracks

event.title: The Sultan's Triumph
event.text: From Aleppo to Aden, the sultan's domain stretches across the ancient heartlands of civilization. Egypt commands the trade routes, the holy cities, and the great crossroads of three continents. No power in the region can match our reach. Yet empire brings choices, shall we forge our dominion into an iron instrument of conquest, maintaining vast armies and imposing our will through sheer military supremacy? Or shall we consolidate our gains, establishing a Pax Aegyptia where Egyptian intelligence and garrisons maintain order while our armies rest?

options.text: Forge the iron fist of the sultan.

modifiers.name: The Iron Sultan
modifiers.text: Egypt's military machine is the terror of the region, vast armies, impregnable fortresses, and an iron will that crushes all opposition, though the cost strains the treasury.

modifiers.name: Pax Aegyptia
modifiers.text: Egyptian intelligence networks and garrison forces maintain order across the sultan's vast domain, ensuring stability through watchfulness rather than conquest, though imperial complacency may yet take root.

destiny.name: Nile's Bounty
destiny.text: Dig the canals and raise the dikes in four places, develop the cotton trade, and transform the Nile valley into an engine of prosperity unmatched in the region.

conditions.text: Chose Garden of the Nile
At least 4 of our locations have Nile Irrigation Works
Gold at least 1000
The capital

Cotton is traded in the market

event.title: The Nile's Promise Fulfilled
event.text: Egyptian cotton now commands premium prices in the markets of the world, and the new canals carry the flood to fields that lay dry for generations. The transformation is remarkable, where once we relied on the sword and the levy, now we build with water, capital and commerce. The Nile's bounty, channeled through dikes and canals, generates wealth that no army alone could seize. Foreign merchants compete for the privilege of trading in our markets, and Egyptian bills of exchange circulate from Venice to Isfahan.

options.text: Prosperity flows as surely as the Nile.

destiny.name: Crossroads of Commerce
destiny.text: Secure the Red Sea coast at Massawa and rebuild Alexandria, the Mediterranean end of the route, to make Egypt the indispensable trade link between Europe and Asia.

conditions.text: Own Massawa, or a subject owns it
We own Alexandria and its development is at least 59
Prestige at least 50

event.title: The Red Sea Question
event.text: With Egypt's trade infrastructure flourishing and the Red Sea coast under our control, we stand at a historic juncture. The commerce flowing between Europe and Asia must pass through our hands, but how shall we profit from this position? We could dominate the sea lanes directly, building a naval presence that controls every vessel from Suez to the Indian Ocean. Or we could focus on the cotton and commodity exchanges, making Egypt the world's indispensable clearing house where Eastern goods meet Western capital. Each approach promises wealth, but of a different character.

options.text: Command the sea lanes from Suez to Aden.

modifiers.name: Master of the Red Sea
modifiers.text: Egypt's naval dominance of the Red Sea ensures that no vessel passes between the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean without Egyptian permission and Egyptian profit.

options.text: Make Egypt the world's cotton exchange.

modifiers.name: Cotton Exchange
modifiers.text: Egyptian cotton commands the world market, and Cairo's commodity exchanges set the prices that merchants from Lisbon to Calcutta must accept.

destiny.name: Jewel of the Orient
destiny.text: Fill the cotton towns and villages with looms and the cane country with presses, and raise Al-Mahalla into a great weaving city, making the Nile valley the most developed and prosperous land between Europe and India.

conditions.text: At least 3 of our locations have a Weaving Hall or a Rural Clothmaker
At least 3 of our locations have a Sugar Press
Gold at least 3000
Prestige at least 75

event.title: The Jewel of the Orient
event.text: Egypt has achieved what few nations dare to dream. Looms in every cotton town, presses along the whole cane country, and wealth that would make the pharaohs envious. The Nile valley hums with work, and new canals carry water to fields that once lay dry through the summer. Now we face the ultimate question: shall Egypt use its wealth and sophistication to project influence outward, reaching toward new horizons with the confidence of a revived civilization? Or shall we turn our gaze to the isthmus of Suez, that narrow strip of land that could, if pierced, transform Egypt into the indispensable link between the oceans of the world?

options.text: Egypt shall reach toward new horizons.

modifiers.name: Pharaoh Reborn
modifiers.text: Egypt reaches outward with the confidence of a revived civilization, projecting influence far beyond the Nile valley, though maintaining such grandeur demands ever greater court expenditure.

options.text: The canal shall unite the seas of the world.

modifiers.name: Vision of Suez
modifiers.text: Egypt transforms itself into the world's indispensable maritime corridor, welcoming ships of every nation through its waters and growing rich on the transit of global commerce.

units.name: Mamluk Ghulam
units.text: Elite slave-soldier cavalry trained from youth in the furusiyya arts of horsemanship, archery, and mounted combat. Their loyalty is to the sultan alone.

units.name: Nile Galley
units.text: A shallow-draft galley designed for patrol and transport along the Nile River and in the coastal waters of the eastern Mediterranean.

units.name: Egyptian Sipahi
units.text: Heavy cavalry lancers combining the Mamluk furusiyya tradition with Ottoman sipahi equipment, devastating in the charge.

units.name: Egyptian Janissary
units.text: Disciplined garrison infantry drilled in Ottoman methods, forming the backbone of Egypt's standing army.

units.name: Felucca
units.text: A fast, lateen-rigged vessel perfectly suited to the Nile, the Red Sea, and the coastal waters of Egypt. Used for patrol, trade, and light combat.

units.name: Nizam-i Jedid
units.text: Soldiers of the New Order, Egyptian infantry trained in European line tactics, drilled to fire by volley and maneuver in formation.

units.name: Egyptian Line Infantry
units.text: Modern professional infantry equipped with percussion-cap muskets and bayonets, organized into European-style brigades.

units.name: Fellahin Conscript
units.text: Egyptian peasant conscripts, numerous but less experienced than professional soldiers. What they lack in training they make up in sheer numbers.

buildings.name: Nile Irrigation Works
buildings.text: Basin irrigation systems, saqiya water wheels, and canal networks that transform the Nile floodplain into the most productive farmland in the region. Built by the river or a lake, on land that grows a winter crop of the flood basins (wheat, beans and lentils, or flax), and raises its harvest.

The location's raw material is Legumes
The location's raw material is Fiber Crops

buildings.name: Sugar Press
buildings.text: A press and boiling house in the cane country. Oxen turn the stones, and the boiled juice sets in clay cones before it is shipped down the Nile. The villages around a press plant all the cane it can take.

where.text: The location's raw material is Sugar

buildings.name: Summer Canal
buildings.text: A canal cut deep enough to carry water when the Nile is low, so that cotton, cane and rice can be watered through the summer. Built on river land that grows one of them. The villages along it are called out each year to clear the silt.

children.text: The location's raw material is Cotton
The location's raw material is Sugar
The location's raw material is Rice

buildings.name: Wikala
buildings.text: An urban caravanserai providing secure lodging, storage, and commercial facilities for merchants traveling the trade routes through Egypt.

buildings.name: Weaving Hall
buildings.text: A hall of looms in a cotton town. The cotton is spun, woven and finished into fine cloth for export.

where.text: Cotton is produced in the location's market

buildings.name: Mamluk Barracks
buildings.text: A training compound where slave soldiers are schooled in the arts of war, emerging as elite cavalry and loyal garrison troops.

buildings.name: Cairo Madrasa
buildings.text: A school of Islamic law and theology endowed by the ruling elite, part of the network of learning centered on Al-Azhar.

buildings.name: Nile Granary
buildings.text: A state granary storing the surplus of the Nile harvest, ensuring food security and enabling grain exports to the Mediterranean.

buildings.name: Red Sea Warehouse
buildings.text: A coastal storage facility for goods in transit between the Red Sea and the Mediterranean, the backbone of Egypt's role as trade intermediary.

buildings.name: Grand Bazaar
buildings.text: A sprawling market complex in the tradition of Khan al-Khalili, where merchants from three continents buy and sell goods under one roof.

buildings.name: Cairo Arsenal
buildings.text: A state weapons manufactory producing muskets, cannons, and gunpowder for the modernized Egyptian army.

buildings.name: State Factory
buildings.text: A government-owned manufacturing facility producing textiles, processed goods, and military equipment as part of Egypt's industrialization program.

buildings.name: Sultan's Citadel
buildings.text: A monumental fortress-palace in the tradition of Saladin's Citadel, serving as the military and administrative heart of the sultan's domain.

buildings.name: Suez Canal Office
buildings.text: A grand administrative complex managing the flow of international commerce through Egypt's transit corridor, the economic engine of the modern Egyptian state.

list.name: Rawk al-Nasiri
list.text: The great land survey of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, carried out by the Army Bureau in Egypt in 1315. Every village was measured and valued and every grant reassigned. The sultan's own share of the land rose from four parts in twenty-four to ten, and from it he paid his royal mamluks. The amirs' grants were cut and scattered across the country so that none held a province together. A crowd of petty taxes on markets and trades was abolished at the same stroke. The bureau's registers fixed what each amir held and what he owed for it.

list.name: Iqta' System
list.text: The military land-grant by which Mamluk amirs received the revenues of provinces in lieu of cash pay, the dominant fiscal-military institution of the sultanate. Unlike the hereditary iqta of earlier dynasties, Mamluk grants were strictly non-hereditary and rotated between holders every few years to prevent local entrenchment. The system supplied a permanent cavalry without the burden of monetary salaries, but in the late Burji period the great amirs increasingly captured the rural fiscal base, pressing the fellahin ever harder and starving the sultanic treasury at Cairo.

list.name: Mamluk Amirate
list.text: The graded hierarchy of mamluk officers: amir of ten (amir ashara), amir of forty (amir tablkhana, who could mount his own kettledrum band), and amir of a hundred and commander of a thousand (muqaddam alf). Each rank carried a fixed contingent of mamluks, a fixed iqta valuation, and a fixed place in the parade order. The system gave the sultanate its army and its officer corps, but the great amirs of a hundred were also the factional kingmakers who deposed and elevated sultans through the Bahri and Burji centuries: a graded aristocracy whose loyalty to the throne was always conditional.

list.name: Al-Azhar
list.text: The great mosque-university of Cairo, founded by the Fatimid general Jawhar al-Siqilli in 970 as a Shi'i institution, then refounded by Saladin in 1171 as a Sunni one and elevated to the foremost center of Sunni scholarship in the world during the Mamluk centuries. Each of the four Sunni schools had its own teaching circle (riwaq) under its own chief mufti; the ulama trained at al-Azhar staffed Egypt's mosques, courts, and madrasas, and through the Ottoman centuries the institution remained the intellectual capital of the Arab world.

conditions.text: Sunnism religion

list.name: Qadi al-Qudat
list.text: The chief judgeship system formalized by Sultan Baybars in 1265, by which Cairo housed not one but four chief qadis, one for each of the Sunni schools of law: Hanafi, Shafi'i, Maliki, and Hanbali. Each chief judge appointed deputies in his madhhab across the realm and presided over inheritance, contract, and family disputes for adherents of his school. The arrangement made Cairo the judicial capital of the Sunni world and gave each madhhab institutional standing, but it also cemented the autonomy of the ulama from sultanic interference and produced jurisdictional rivalries that occasionally paralyzed the courts.

conditions.text: Sunnism religion

list.name: Diwan al-Aqbat
list.text: The longstanding employment of Coptic Christian clerks in the fiscal bureaus of Egypt, a tradition reaching back to the Abbasid kharaj registers and surviving every change of dynasty. Coptic secretarial dynasties held the practical knowledge of land assessment, revenue accounting, and surveying that successive Muslim regimes could not easily replace; one Hibat Allah al-Sadid even rose to mustawfi al-suhba (chief comptroller) under Qalawun. Their continuity was punctuated by at least nine documented purges between the late thirteenth and mid-fifteenth centuries (triggered by mob pressure or sultanic favor), but the clerks were always restored when the registers fell into chaos.

list.name: Bread Price of Cairo
list.text: In Cairo the market inspector had one duty above all the others: the price of bread. He set what a loaf could cost in a city of half a million, watched the grain boats unload, and answered for it when the Nile failed. In 1394 the people of Cairo went to the vice-sultan to blame the inspector for dear grain. The historian al-Maqrizi took the office in 1399. The inspector's fixed prices set him against the amirs who hoarded grain and against the peasants whose crop he valued cheap.

conditions.text: Owns Cairo
